prompt: What is the page tree that scripts work with?
optionA: The file that was delivered from the server
optionB: The browser's live in-memory representation of the page
optionC: A browser option that has to be switched on
optionD: Something supplied by a framework
correctAnswerText: The browser's live in-memory representation of the page
explanation: Scripts work on the browser's live in-memory representation of the page, which the browser keeps for as long as the page is open. The delivered file is only what it was built from.

prompt: Where does that tree come from?
optionA: It is downloaded from the server as a second file
optionB: The developer writes it alongside the markup
optionC: It is created only when a script first asks for it
optionD: The browser builds it from the delivered markup
correctAnswerText: The browser builds it from the delivered markup
explanation: The browser builds it from the delivered markup as the page is read, before any script runs. Nothing extra is fetched and nothing has to be requested.

prompt: Once a page has finished loading, can that tree still be changed?
optionA: Yes, for as long as the page stays open
optionB: No; it is fixed until the page is reloaded
optionC: No; it can be read but never changed
optionD: Only while the page is still loading
correctAnswerText: Yes, for as long as the page stays open
explanation: The tree stays available and changeable for as long as the page stays open, which is what makes interactive pages possible at all. Loading finishing is not a freeze.

prompt: Does a plain script on a page need a library before it can reach the page tree?
optionA: Yes; a library is required
optionB: Yes, unless a framework is used instead
optionC: No; reaching it is part of the browser itself
optionD: Only for changing it, not for reading it
correctAnswerText: No; reaching it is part of the browser itself
explanation: Reaching the tree is part of the browser itself, so a plain script can already read and change it. Libraries make the same work shorter to write rather than possible.

prompt: A script inserts a new paragraph into the page. The developer then asks the browser to show the page source. Is the new paragraph in what they see?
optionA: Yes; the source is kept in step with the page
optionB: No; the source shown is the delivered file, which the script never touched
optionC: Yes, but only after the page is reloaded
optionD: No; the paragraph was never really added
correctAnswerText: No; the source shown is the delivered file, which the script never touched
explanation: The paragraph is genuinely in the live page and not in the delivered file, so the source shown is the delivered file, which the script never touched. Inspecting the live tree shows the paragraph; viewing the source does not.

prompt: A lookup by identifier finds a matching element. What does the lookup produce?
optionA: A collection containing that one element
optionB: The text inside that element
optionC: True, to say it was found
optionD: That one element
correctAnswerText: That one element
explanation: A lookup by identifier produces that one element, ready to be read or changed directly. No collection is involved, so no position has to be taken from it.

prompt: A lookup for every element carrying a class matches three elements. What does the lookup produce?
optionA: A collection of the three elements
optionB: The first of the three elements
optionC: The three elements joined into one piece of text
optionD: The number of matches
correctAnswerText: A collection of the three elements
explanation: A lookup for every match produces a collection of the three elements, whatever the number of matches turns out to be. Reaching any one of them means taking it out of the collection first.

prompt: A lookup by identifier matches nothing. What happens?
optionA: It throws an error and the program stops
optionB: It produces an empty collection
optionC: It produces null and the program carries on
optionD: It produces the closest matching element instead
correctAnswerText: It produces null and the program carries on
explanation: A failed lookup produces null and the program carries on, which is why the failure is only noticed on the next line. Nothing is raised at the lookup itself.

prompt: One lookup asks for a single element and another asks for every match. Neither finds anything. How do the two results differ?
optionA: Both give null
optionB: The single lookup gives null and the every-match lookup gives an empty collection
optionC: Both give an empty collection
optionD: Both raise the same error
correctAnswerText: The single lookup gives null and the every-match lookup gives an empty collection
explanation: The two failures are shaped differently: the single lookup gives null and the every-match lookup gives an empty collection. That is why one crashes on the next line and the other quietly loops zero times.

prompt: A click handler is attached while the page is loading. Has the code inside it run at that point?
optionA: Yes; attaching runs it once
optionB: Yes, and it will also run on each click
optionC: Only once the page has been reloaded
optionD: No; it runs when a click happens
correctAnswerText: No; it runs when a click happens
explanation: Attaching only records what should happen later, so the code inside runs when a click happens and not before. Nothing about the attaching itself executes the body.

prompt: A button carrying one handler is clicked three times. How many times does the handler run?
optionA: Three times
optionB: Once, after which it stops listening
optionC: Once per page load, however many clicks occur
optionD: Never, unless it is attached again after each click
correctAnswerText: Three times
explanation: A handler stays attached and answers every click, so it runs three times. Nothing detaches it after the first.

prompt: A handler is attached and the user never clicks the element. What becomes of the code inside it?
optionA: It runs once when the page finishes loading
optionB: It runs when the user leaves the page
optionC: It never runs
optionD: It runs after a short delay
correctAnswerText: It never runs
explanation: Code inside a handler waits for its event and nothing else triggers it, so it never runs. There is no fallback moment at which it is executed anyway.

prompt: A script attaches a click handler and then prints a line. The user clicks a second later. In what order do the printing and the handler run?
optionA: The handler first, because handlers take priority
optionB: The printing first, because attaching does not wait for anything
optionC: They run at the same moment
optionD: The printing is held back until the click arrives
correctAnswerText: The printing first, because attaching does not wait for anything
explanation: Attaching finishes immediately and the script continues, so the printing happens first, because attaching does not wait for anything. The handler runs a second later when the click actually arrives.

prompt:
The page contains

A

B

. A lookup asks for a single element matching .note. Which is produced?
optionA: The paragraph containing B, as the last match
optionB: Both paragraphs, as a collection
optionC: null, because more than one element matches
optionD: The paragraph containing A
correctAnswerText: The paragraph containing A
explanation: A single-element lookup takes the first match in document order, which is the paragraph containing A. Extra matches are ignored rather than causing a failure.

prompt:
The page contains
X
followed by Y. A lookup asks for every element matching #box .tag. How many are found, and which?
optionA: One: the span containing X
optionB: Two: both spans
optionC: One: the span containing Y
optionD: None, because the span is not a direct child
correctAnswerText: One: the span containing X
explanation: The lookup is limited to what sits inside the identified element, so it finds one: the span containing X. The second span carries the same class but sits outside.

prompt:
The page contains

Hello there

. What does reading the paragraph's text produce?
optionA: Hello there
optionB: Hello
optionC: Hello there
optionD: there
correctAnswerText: Hello there
explanation: Reading the text gives the words with the tags stripped out and the nested words kept, which is Hello there. The nested element contributes its words but not its tags.

prompt:
The page contains
  • Price: 99
    • . What does reading the item's markup produce?
optionA: Price: 99
optionB: Price: 99
optionC: Price:
optionD: • Price: 99
correctAnswerText: Price: 99
explanation: Reading the markup gives everything between the opening and closing tags exactly as it stands, which is Price: 99. The element's own tags are not part of what is inside it.

prompt: A script sets a heading's text to Welcome. Who sees the change?
optionA: Everyone who loads the page from now on
optionB: Everyone, once the server has caught up
optionC: Nobody, until the change is saved
optionD: Only this visitor, in this browser, on this open page
correctAnswerText: Only this visitor, in this browser, on this open page
explanation: The change is made to the copy of the page held in one browser, so only this visitor, in this browser, on this open page sees it. Nothing was sent anywhere.

prompt: After a script has changed a heading, the visitor reloads the page. What heading appears?
optionA: The original one, because the page is built again from the delivered markup
optionB: The changed one, which survives reloads
optionC: No heading at all
optionD: The changed one, until the browser cache is cleared
correctAnswerText: The original one, because the page is built again from the delivered markup
explanation: A reload throws the live tree away and builds a new one, so the original one appears, because the page is built again from the delivered markup. The script would have to run again to change it again.

prompt: A student is sure their form saves data, because after clicking Save the entered values are still on the screen. Their Save handler only writes the values into the page. They reload and everything is gone. What does the reload demonstrate?
optionA: That the save worked but the server has not caught up
optionB: That reloading deleted what had been saved
optionC: That nothing ever left the browser; only the live page had been changed
optionD: That the browser cache was cleared at the wrong moment
correctAnswerText: That nothing ever left the browser; only the live page had been changed
explanation: Values staying on screen prove only that the live page holds them, and the reload rebuilds the page from the delivered markup: nothing ever left the browser; only the live page had been changed. Saving requires sending the values somewhere that outlives the page.

prompt: A stylesheet contains .hidden { display: none; }. A script adds the class hidden to a paragraph that is currently on screen. What happens to it?
optionA: It stays, because the sheet had already been applied when the script ran
optionB: It disappears from view
optionC: It disappears once the page is reloaded
optionD: It stays, because a script cannot bring a sheet rule into play
correctAnswerText: It disappears from view
explanation: Which rules match is worked out again every time the page changes, so the paragraph now matches and It disappears from view. Sheets are not applied once at the start and then forgotten.

prompt: A stylesheet contains #save { color: red; } and .btn { color: blue; }. A script adds the class btn to the element whose identifier is save. What colour is the element?
optionA: Blue, because the class was added most recently
optionB: Blue, because a change made by a script outranks the stylesheet
optionC: Neither; the two rules cancel each other
optionD: Red, because the identifier rule is the more specific of the two
correctAnswerText: Red, because the identifier rule is the more specific of the two
explanation: The element now matches both rules and the cascade settles it on specificity, so it stays red, because the identifier rule is the more specific of the two. When the class was added makes no difference.

prompt: A stylesheet sets an element's colour to red through its identifier. A script sets the colour to green on the element itself. The element shows green, even though an identifier rule is highly specific. Why?
optionA: A style set on the element itself is considered after every stylesheet rule
optionB: Because the script ran later in time than the stylesheet
optionC: Because a script always overrides a stylesheet
optionD: Because green is applied to the text and red to the background
correctAnswerText: A style set on the element itself is considered after every stylesheet rule
explanation: What the script produced is not another stylesheet rule but a style on the element, and a style set on the element itself is considered after every stylesheet rule. Running later is not the reason: a stylesheet loaded afterwards would still lose.

prompt: Three buttons each receive their own handler, and each handler hides the element that was clicked. The second button is clicked. What happens?
optionA: All three buttons are hidden
optionB: The first button is hidden
optionC: The second button is hidden
optionD: Nothing happens
correctAnswerText: The second button is hidden
explanation: Each handler acts on whatever was clicked, so the second button is hidden and the others are untouched. The click decides the target.

prompt: Three similar buttons exist, but a handler was attached to the first one only. The third button is clicked. What happens?
optionA: The first button is hidden
optionB: Nothing, because the third button has no handler
optionC: The third button is hidden
optionD: All three buttons are hidden
correctAnswerText: Nothing, because the third button has no handler
explanation: A handler only answers clicks on the element it was attached to, so nothing happens, because the third button has no handler. Attaching to one element does not cover its lookalikes.

prompt: Every button in a list has a handler attached, and clicking any of them always hides the first button. What is the fault?
optionA: Only the first button actually received a handler
optionB: The handlers were attached before the buttons existed
optionC: All the buttons share one identifier
optionD: The handler acts on a fixed element instead of the one that was clicked
correctAnswerText: The handler acts on a fixed element instead of the one that was clicked
explanation: Something happens on every click, so every button really is wired up and the attaching timing is fine; what is wrong is that the handler acts on a fixed element instead of the one that was clicked. The handler needs the clicked element rather than a name resolved once.

prompt: A script is placed above the markup it looks up and runs as soon as it is reached. Does the lookup find the element?
optionA: No; that part of the page has not been built yet
optionB: Yes; the browser waits for the whole page first
optionC: Yes; lookups search the delivered file rather than the page
optionD: Only when the lookup uses an identifier
correctAnswerText: No; that part of the page has not been built yet
explanation: The page is built from the top downwards and the script runs where it sits, so no, that part of the page has not been built yet. The lookup searches the live tree, which is still incomplete.

prompt: The same script is moved below the markup it looks up. Does the lookup find the element now?
optionA: No; where a script sits makes no difference
optionB: Only after the page is reloaded once
optionC: Yes; the element has been built by the time the script runs
optionD: Only if it also waits for the page to finish loading
correctAnswerText: Yes; the element has been built by the time the script runs
explanation: Everything above a script exists before the script runs, so yes, the element has been built by the time the script runs. Waiting for a load event is another way to get the same guarantee, not a further requirement.

prompt: A lookup gives null when the page loads. Typing exactly the same lookup into the console afterwards finds the element. What is the cause?
optionA: The selector does not match the element
optionB: The script ran before that element had been built
optionC: The element is hidden by a stylesheet rule
optionD: The browser does not support that kind of lookup
correctAnswerText: The script ran before that element had been built
explanation: The console result proves the selector matches and the element exists, so the only thing that differs between the two attempts is when they happened: the script ran before that element had been built.

prompt: A lookup returns the three elements carrying a class. The script then sets a style on the returned collection itself. What happens on the page?
optionA: All three elements change
optionB: The first element changes
optionC: An error stops the script
optionD: Nothing changes
correctAnswerText: Nothing changes
explanation: A collection is a list of elements and not an element, so setting a style on it changes nothing on the page. No error is raised either, which is what makes this hard to spot.

prompt: How is a style applied to every element in such a collection?
optionA: By going through the collection and setting the style on each element in turn
optionB: By setting the style on the collection once
optionC: By setting the style on the first element, which the rest follow
optionD: By running the lookup again for each element
correctAnswerText: By going through the collection and setting the style on each element in turn
explanation: The collection holds the elements but is not one of them, so the work is done by going through the collection and setting the style on each element in turn. There is no shortcut that reaches them all at once.

prompt: A script sets a style on a collection and nothing changes, with no error reported. A colleague says the selector must be wrong. What single check settles which of the two it is?
optionA: Reload the page and try again
optionB: Set the style on the first element instead
optionC: Print how many elements the collection holds
optionD: Try a different style property
correctAnswerText: Print how many elements the collection holds
explanation: A wrong selector and a style set on the collection look identical from outside, and they differ in exactly one observable: print how many elements the collection holds. Zero means the selector, three means the collection was styled instead of its members.

prompt: A control declared to accept numbers holds 20. A script reads its value and compares it with the number 20 using the strict form of equality. What is the result?
optionA: True, because both are 20
optionB: False, because the value read out is text
optionC: True, but only because the control accepts numbers
optionD: An error, because the two types cannot be compared
correctAnswerText: False, because the value read out is text
explanation: A control hands back what the user typed as text whatever the control is declared to accept, so the comparison is false, because the value read out is text. The strict form refuses to convert before comparing.

prompt: A script checks a text control against undefined to see whether the user typed nothing. The user types nothing and the check still never matches. Why?
optionA: The control was not found by the lookup
optionB: The value is null rather than undefined
optionC: The check has to use the converting form of equality
optionD: An untouched control gives an empty string, which is not undefined
correctAnswerText: An untouched control gives an empty string, which is not undefined
explanation: A control always has a value and it starts as text with no characters in it, so an untouched control gives an empty string, which is not undefined. Checking the length, or comparing against an empty string, is what detects it.

prompt:
The page contains

X

. Starting from the paragraph, which element is its parent?
optionA: The section
optionB: The div
optionC: The paragraph itself
optionD: The body
correctAnswerText: The section
explanation: The section is the parent, because a parent is the element that directly contains another. The div contains that section and is therefore one level further out.

prompt: The page contains a list written across several lines, with each item on its own line. Asking the first item for its next element sibling gives the second item. Asking it for its next node instead often gives something else. What?
optionA: The list itself
optionB: The second item again, by another route
optionC: The whitespace text sitting between the two items
optionD: Nothing, in every case
correctAnswerText: The whitespace text sitting between the two items
explanation: Line breaks and indentation between tags are themselves content in the tree, so the next node is the whitespace text sitting between the two items. Asking specifically for elements is what skips it.

prompt: A lookup written with the class name but without a leading dot finds nothing, although elements carrying that class exist and the script runs late enough. What is wrong?
optionA: The script still runs too early
optionB: The selector is being read as an element name rather than a class
optionC: The class is spelled differently in the markup
optionD: A class can only be found through a collection lookup
correctAnswerText: The selector is being read as an element name rather than a class
explanation: Without the dot the text names a kind of element, and no element is called that, so the selector is being read as an element name rather than a class. Adding the dot is the whole fix.

prompt: A lookup gives null. The script sits at the bottom of the page and runs after the markup, and the same selector typed into the console afterwards also finds nothing. What is the cause?
optionA: The script ran before the element existed
optionB: The element is hidden by a stylesheet rule
optionC: The page failed to finish loading
optionD: The selector matches nothing in the page
correctAnswerText: The selector matches nothing in the page
explanation: Timing is ruled out twice over, by the script's position and by the console attempt made after loading, so the selector matches nothing in the page. A hidden element would still be found.

prompt: Two causes give the same null lookup: the script ran too early, or the selector matches nothing. Which single check separates them?
optionA: Run the same lookup in the console once the page has finished loading
optionB: Reload the page and watch whether it happens again
optionC: Move the script to the bottom of the page
optionD: Add a short wait before the lookup
correctAnswerText: Run the same lookup in the console once the page has finished loading
explanation: The two causes differ only in whether the element exists at lookup time, so run the same lookup in the console once the page has finished loading and the answer is immediate. Moving the script or adding a wait would fix one cause without ever showing which it was.

prompt: Moving a script to the bottom of the page makes a failing lookup start working. What has that established?
optionA: That the selector was wrong and has now been corrected
optionB: Nothing; the change could have fixed anything
optionC: That timing was the cause, and the selector was correct all along
optionD: That the element was hidden and is now visible
correctAnswerText: That timing was the cause, and the selector was correct all along
explanation: Only when the script runs changed, and the outcome changed with it, so timing was the cause, and the selector was correct all along. A wrong selector would still find nothing from the bottom of the page.

prompt: A lookup works on the developer's page and gives null on another page built from the same template, where that element is only rendered when there is data to show. What is the likeliest cause?
optionA: The script runs earlier on that page
optionB: On that page the element genuinely is not there
optionC: The selector is wrong and only appeared to work
optionD: That page loads the script from a different place
correctAnswerText: On that page the element genuinely is not there
explanation: The stem gives a condition under which the element is left out entirely, and the failing page is the one meeting it, so on that page the element genuinely is not there. The code is the same on both pages; the data is not.

prompt: A handler was attached by writing the function name followed by parentheses. Its message appears once while the page is loading, and clicking afterwards does nothing. What happened?
optionA: The handler was attached to the wrong element
optionB: The element did not exist when the attaching ran
optionC: Another element sits on top and swallows the clicks
optionD: The function was run at that moment and what it returned was attached instead of the function
correctAnswerText: The function was run at that moment and what it returned was attached instead of the function
explanation: The parentheses call the function there and then, which is why the message appeared during loading: the function was run at that moment and what it returned was attached instead of the function. Dropping the parentheses attaches the function itself.

prompt: Three faults all end with nothing happening on click: the handler was called instead of referenced, the element did not exist when the attaching ran, and the handler was attached to a collection. Which of them leaves a visible trace while the page loads?
optionA: The one that called the handler, because its body runs once immediately
optionB: The one attached before the element existed
optionC: The one attached to a collection
optionD: None of them leaves a trace
correctAnswerText: The one that called the handler, because its body runs once immediately
explanation: Two of the faults do nothing observable at attach time, while calling the function runs it: the one that called the handler, because its body runs once immediately, is the one that shows. That single early trace is what separates it from the other two without reading the code.

prompt: Nothing happens on click, and the console shows an error at the attaching line saying a property cannot be read of null. Which of the three faults is it?
optionA: The handler was called instead of referenced
optionB: The handler was attached to a collection
optionC: The element did not exist when the attaching ran
optionD: The body of the handler has a fault in it
correctAnswerText: The element did not exist when the attaching ran
explanation: A failed lookup gives null, and attaching to null is what raises that error at that line, so the element did not exist when the attaching ran. A fault inside the body could not report itself before any click.

prompt: Nothing happens on click, no error appears anywhere, and nothing ran while the page was loading. Which of the three faults fits?
optionA: The handler was called instead of referenced
optionB: The handler was attached to a collection rather than to its members
optionC: The element did not exist when the attaching ran
optionD: All three fit this description equally
correctAnswerText: The handler was attached to a collection rather than to its members
explanation: Calling the handler would have left a trace during loading and attaching to null would have raised an error, so the silence on both counts points at the remaining one: the handler was attached to a collection rather than to its members. Attaching to a collection succeeds and reaches nothing.

prompt: A table of fifty rows can be wired up by attaching a handler to each row, or by attaching one handler to the table and working out which row was clicked. What does the single handler cost?
optionA: Nothing; it is better in every respect
optionB: It stops working as soon as rows are added
optionC: It runs once for every row on each click
optionD: It has to work out the row itself, and gets that wrong when the markup inside a row changes
correctAnswerText: It has to work out the row itself, and gets that wrong when the markup inside a row changes
explanation: The single handler is cheaper to attach and keeps working for rows added later, and the price is that it has to work out the row itself, and gets that wrong when the markup inside a row changes. Fifty handlers know their row without asking.

prompt: A row must be shown as selected. Replacing the row's markup and adding a class to the existing row both produce the right appearance. Which has the fewest side effects?
optionA: Adding the class, because replacing the markup throws away the handlers attached to that row
optionB: Replacing the markup, because it keeps the change in one place
optionC: They are identical in effect
optionD: Replacing the markup, because a class can be overridden by the stylesheet
correctAnswerText: Adding the class, because replacing the markup throws away the handlers attached to that row
explanation: Both look right, so the choice is decided by what else changes: adding the class, because replacing the markup throws away the handlers attached to that row. New elements start with nothing attached to them.

prompt: One item in a list of two hundred has changed. Rebuilding the whole list and updating that one item both end with the right list on screen. What does rebuilding cost?
optionA: Nothing; the two are equivalent
optionB: It stops working once the list is long enough
optionC: The other items are discarded and remade, losing focus, scroll position and attached handlers
optionD: It changes the order the items appear in
correctAnswerText: The other items are discarded and remade, losing focus, scroll position and attached handlers
explanation: The screen ends up the same either way, and the difference is in what was destroyed on the way there: the other items are discarded and remade, losing focus, scroll position and attached handlers. Rebuilding is simpler to write, which is why it is chosen.

prompt: A message needs part of it in bold. Setting the paragraph's text to a string containing bold tags shows the tags as literal characters on screen. Why?
optionA: A bold element is not allowed inside a paragraph
optionB: Setting text treats everything given as characters rather than as markup
optionC: The stylesheet has removed the bolding
optionD: The text was set before the paragraph existed
correctAnswerText: Setting text treats everything given as characters rather than as markup
explanation: The two ways of putting content into an element differ exactly here: setting text treats everything given as characters rather than as markup. Setting markup instead is what would produce a bold word.

prompt: Something a user typed has to be shown back to them. Which way of putting it into the page should be preferred, and why?
optionA: Setting markup, because it is the more flexible of the two
optionB: Either; what appears on screen is the same
optionC: Setting markup, because text cannot show punctuation
optionD: Setting text, because interpreting what a user typed as markup lets it bring behaviour with it
correctAnswerText: Setting text, because interpreting what a user typed as markup lets it bring behaviour with it
explanation: The safe default is setting text, because interpreting what a user typed as markup lets it bring behaviour with it. The two only look interchangeable while the input is well behaved.
